tagline: A river gorge connects Bat Cave, Chimney Rock and Lake Lure
intro: Black Mountain Rag appears in North Carolina’s scenic-byways guidebook. The road corridor runs from Black Mountain on NC 9 to Bat Cave, where it joins US 64 and US 74A in Hickory Nut Gorge. The Broad River passes through Bat Cave; farther along are Chimney Rock’s 315-foot gneiss monolith and the lake created by damming the river at Lake Lure. Bat Cave and Chimney Rock lie within a narrow gorge with steep walls.

A drovers’ road established in 1798 connected the Bat Cave area with Asheville along the corridor now followed by US 74A. Drovers moved turkeys, geese, hogs and cattle between the mountains and markets. In the 1920s, the Morse family’s dam project reshaped the Broad River into Lake Lure, completing the impoundment in 1927.

The geographic sequence is Black Mountain, Bat Cave, Chimney Rock and Lake Lure. At Bat Cave, the three highways merge as Lake Lure Highway and continue southeast. Helene flooding damaged Bat Cave, Chimney Rock and Lake Lure in 2024.

moments.title: Bat Cave
moments.text: Bat Cave takes its name from a cave on Bluerock Mountain, a protected place closed to the public. The community sits beside the Broad River where NC 9, US 64 and US 74A merge. Its post office moved here and took the Bat Cave name in 1879, after earlier service as the Chimney Rock Post Office. Flooding destroyed the post office and much of the community in 1916; the post office was rebuilt. Tourism grew in the 1920s; the 186-acre Bat Cave Preserve was established to protect the cave’s bats, including endangered Indiana bats. Helene brought significant damage again in 2024.

moments.title: Chimney Rock
moments.text: Chimney Rock is a 315-foot monolith of gneiss, shaped by erosion along joints in the rock. Large blocks break away from rock surfaces and fall or slide, processes that have produced fissure caves in the gorge. Lucius B. Morse bought 64 acres here in 1902, including the Chimney and cliffs. His family ran the park privately until 2007, when the state completed its purchase agreement. The state park also contains the 404-foot Hickory Nut Falls. Helene destroyed the park’s access bridge in 2024; the park reopened on June 27, 2025.

moments.title: Lake Lure
moments.text: Lake Lure began as a dam project financed through a mortgage. The Morse family formed Carolina Mountain Power Company in 1925, and the Broad River impoundment was complete in 1927. The power plant began selling electricity the following year. Elizabeth Morse, Lucius’s wife, is credited with naming both lake and town. When the Depression halted development, Philadelphia mortgage-holder Stroud & Company foreclosed on the lake and dam. The town acquired the dam, power company and real estate in 1965. Flooding during Helene damaged the town and the dam’s structural supports in September 2024, though its wall remained stable.
